title: 88% of Young Americans Admit to Doomscrolling
paragraphs: "Doomscrolling" means spending a long time online reading through bad news and upsetting content — which can have a real impact on our mental health.
And according to a survey by research organizations Hopelab and Data for Progress, 88% of young people in the US do it at least sometimes.
The survey included almost 1,500 young people aged 13 to 24, and it also found that 32% doomscroll once or even a few times a day.
A lot of young people said they doomscroll in bed, either before sleep or in the morning before getting up.

One-third of the survey participants said they lose more than an hour of sleep on nights when they doomscroll. Twenty-five percent said they lose 30 minutes to an hour of sleep to doomscrolling, and 18% lose 15 to 30 minutes.
And for 60% of participants, doomscrolling makes them feel anxious, overwhelmed, angry, hopeless or mentally exhausted.

There is another side, though, as 76% said that doomscrolling helped them feel informed about issues. Sixty percent also said it made them want to take action, like changing their own behavior, donating or getting involved in activism.

In August, Meta, which owns social media platforms like Facebook and Instagram, agreed to pay an $18 billion settlement to 48 US states, Washington, DC, and three other US territories over claims its platforms harmed children.
The case has also led to new child safety tools for Meta's platforms in those regions, including limits on notifications during school hours, and on how long and when teens can use the platforms.
However, Hopelab has warned against rules that just tell young people to disconnect, because so many of them reported feeling informed and inspired by things they saw on social media.
It did, however, encourage young people to avoid doomscrolling before bed, and to find other ways to learn about issues that won't lead to them reading upsetting content for hours at a time.
